name: Hassan Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I unlock the storage cage at the Hill Park school extension, count the door frames and help the lead carpenter set them. I'm fifty-eight and junior because I came to building work late after a long spell driving buses; I left school before finishing. My partner Lydia still works at the bus depot office, and our two children are grown. The builder's site rate is good and we've saved roughly fourteen months of expenses. I like the exactness of a door that swings cleanly, but I still ask the lead to check my hinge marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little software may tidy the stores list, but somebody still has to look at the actual stack. I'd keep the same work habits if jobs and prices stay much as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage feels secure on the school extension, and Lydia's depot wages are steady. We have a long enough reserve and several builders nearby, so this picture does not shake our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll count the frames myself each morning and keep setting doors with lead carpenter Emil. In the first year I'd continue the usual savings transfer and ask him to tell me if any stores form changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm; this sounds close to what we already do. I'd rather spend my energy getting the fire doors right than talking about a small computer change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the physical count so important?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delivery docket can say six doors when only five have come off the lorry. If nobody walks to the cage, the missing door becomes tomorrow's delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a phone tool for the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI tools and I have no need to start for a routine count. If the firm changes the form, Emil can show me the new boxes.

say: I'd say **stores software** cannot replace checking the actual stack.
I'd expect the same **door work** if jobs and prices stay steady.
think: My **site wage** and Lydia's depot income look secure.
Our **fourteen-month reserve** and many local builders make modest change manageable.
do: Count **door frames** in the cage each morning.
Keep setting **school doors** and making the usual savings transfer.
feel: **Calm** about small software changes, focused on fire-door accuracy.
S0.quote: If nobody walks to the cage, the missing door becomes tomorrow's delay.
fieldNote: Hassan anchors his scepticism in a **missing delivery** that paperwork could not resolve.
His **strong reserve**, dual wages and local builders make the plateau financially quiet for him.

steps.text: Keep counting and setting doors on the Hill Park site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At tea break I'd say faster buying is useful only if the doors arrive on the day we can fit them. I would ask the manager to show the next job calendar before promising that software will make us busier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Estimates and buying could be done by fewer office people, and I could end up with an empty week between sites. I have money to cover a gap, but I'm still a junior carpenter and not the first person a foreman keeps when work slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the school job and ask Emil when the next contract starts. If the calendar shows a gap, I'll take my paper record of finished rooms to two nearby builders and ask about real vacancies; I won't buy a course from someone selling a quick fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than frightened. A lost week would annoy me, but our household could carry it while I looked for another site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in the paper record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school rooms I helped finish, dates, and Emil's sign-off where he has given one. I need proof because I've only been a carpenter a short time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long a gap would make you apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a full month was blank, I would start making calls before the site closes. A short delivery delay is different from no next contract.

say: I'd ask for the **next job calendar** before praising faster buying.
I'd judge software by whether **doors arrive** when fitters need them.
think: Fewer office staff could mean an **empty site week** for me.
My **junior standing** matters more than the size of our reserve if contracts dry up.
do: Ask Emil for the **next contract** date.
Keep a **room record** and contact nearby builders after a blank month.
feel: **Watchful**, but able to cover a short gap while searching.
S1.quote: A short delivery delay is different from no next contract.
fieldNote: His **paper room record** compensates for short trade experience, even though he avoids new AI tools.
A blank **contract month** triggers applications; he distinguishes that risk from an ordinary delivery delay.

steps.text: Keep taking paid door work at Hill Park
Contact two nearby builders after a blank contract month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thinking system in 2028 may change drawings and schedules first, but the fire doors still need fitting until robots can do site work around 2031. I would ask the boss for straight dates rather than a speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty, I might still have paid work even if the office changes. At sixty-three, a capable robot could take the door fitting; fourteen months saved would buy time, but losing the higher wage before Lydia and I settle retirement would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll put more of each full week's pay into our reserve and gather Emil's signed room sheets. In 2029 I'd keep accepting paid site shifts if they exist, and I would apply to local builders if the roster fell below three days; I won't leave a paying job just because a card names a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the 2031 site change, not helpless. I know where I can ask for work, but I do not know how many builders would still need juniors then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use three days as your line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three days covers our ordinary bills with Lydia's wage, but it stops us adding much to savings. If the roster fell that far, I would need to know whether another employer could give me full weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when the robot arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Lydia and I had the figures to live on without my pay. A robot date is not a retirement fund.

say: I'd separate **2028 office change** from 2031 robot door fitting.
I'd ask for **straight site dates** from the boss.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot fitting could remove my higher wage.
Our **fourteen-month reserve** buys time but does not settle retirement.
do: Save more from **full weeks** and collect signed room sheets.
Apply to **local builders** if the roster falls below three days.
feel: **Anxious** about site wage loss, with a clear job-search threshold.
S2.quote: A robot date is not a retirement fund.
fieldNote: Hassan's **three-day threshold** links a job search to actual household bills and saving capacity.
He places the main income risk at the **2031 robot date**, while admitting local junior demand is uncertain.

steps.text: Set aside more pay after full site weeks
Keep taking paid fire-door shifts in 2029
Apply to local builders if shifts fall below three days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Emil five years should be enough to see whether the new site machines actually work. I would want a written work schedule and proper safety checks before anyone replaces a door crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI comes and sixty-six when robots might fit doors. Lydia and I may be able to ease into retirement by then, but we have not priced health costs and living expenses that far out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working the school and later sites and save extra from full months. In 2032 I'd take paid door jobs if offered and ask the manager to show the next schedule; if the list of jobs dries up, I'd apply to another builder while I can still show recent work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed than in the two-year case. A few years of wages could make the choice to stop real, but I won't spend money we haven't earned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proper safety checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person should inspect the frame and be able to stop the equipment before someone is hurt. I'd read a plain safety report if the company produced one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn to operate the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never used AI tools, and I wouldn't sign up for machine training on a sales claim. If a safe paid role opened, I would look at its terms then.

say: I'd ask for a **written schedule** and site safety checks.
I'd wait to see **working machines** before making a claim about replacement.
think: At **sixty-six**, robot fitting may arrive as retirement approaches.
Our **future expenses** remain unknown, so I cannot promise to stop working.
do: Keep **paid door work** and save extra from full months.
Check the **2032 schedule** and apply elsewhere if site jobs dry up.
feel: Less **pressed**, while I avoid spending wages we have not earned.
S3.quote: I won't spend money we haven't earned.
fieldNote: The five-year path gives Hassan **more pay periods** before robot site work, reducing immediate distress.
He will read a **plain safety report** but declines speculative machine training and keeps retirement conditional.

steps.text: Keep taking paid door jobs through 2032 if offered
Save extra after full paid months
Apply to another builder if the site schedule empties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to keep earning and to make sense of the figures at home. I would still expect the employer to show workers what site robots can do before placing one beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots could fit doors. I may already have stopped climbing site stairs, yet I might still need paid light repairs if Lydia and I have not saved enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking door work while my knees allow and put extra aside from full months. In 2037 I'd take paid ground-floor repair calls if we need wages, and Lydia and I would total our savings and bills before I leave work altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the technology being that far away. What matters now is keeping my health and a clean work record through the years I can still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your adult children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own rent and families; I would not write my grown children's pay into our budget. We can talk with them, but I want our plan to stand on our own numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would end your site work sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A doctor telling me the stairs were no longer safe would make me seek ground-floor jobs. I would stop earning entirely only after Lydia and I saw what income remained.

say: I'd say ten years allows **more earnings** and a careful home budget.
I'd expect the employer to **demonstrate robots** before site use.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid light work.
At **seventy-one**, retirement depends on real savings and Lydia's income.
do: Keep **door work** while my knees allow and save extra.
Take **ground-floor repairs** in 2037 if money is needed.
Review **bills and savings** with Lydia before leaving paid work.
feel: **Calm** about distant robots, focused on health and current earnings.
S4.quote: I would not write my grown children's pay into our budget.
fieldNote: Hassan treats the long robot date as **time to earn**, without claiming guaranteed retirement.
His **stairs and knees** may limit work before technology does, while adult children's income stays outside the plan.

steps.text: Keep taking paid door work while fit
Put extra aside after full site months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most, because a robot could reach my door fitting by sixty-three. Written site dates, a fair notice period and actual paid openings nearby would let me look for work before savings become the only income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a new machine is faster after you count the time spent checking and correcting it. I want the whole job measured, not just a tidy demonstration.

headlineQuote: A delivery docket can say six doors when only five have come off the lorry.
portrait: Hassan is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter who entered site work after bus driving.
His higher site rate, Lydia's wages and **fourteen months saved** give him a strong buffer.
He has **never used AI** and relies on physical counts, signed room sheets and written schedules.
He would keep **paid work** and seek other local builders if site hours fall sharply.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could reach his hands-on door fitting around 2031, before retirement figures are settled.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written site dates**, fair notice and real nearby paid vacancies.
